questions.stem: An 81 year old man who is obese and mostly chair-bound has a 4 month history of an ulcer on his left lower leg. It is shallow, oozing and has irregular edges, and lies just above the medial malleolus. It is only mildly sore. Foot pulses are palpable and his ABPI is 1.04. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 80 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A shallow, exudative, mildly painful ulcer above the medial malleolus with a normal ABPI is a venous ulcer, the commonest leg ulcer; arterial ulcers are painful and punched-out with a low ABPI.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Immobility and obesity cause venous stasis; a shallow exudative gaiter ulcer that is only mildly painful with a normal ABPI is venous.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous ulcer.

elim: Painful, punched-out, over the toes or pressure points, with a low ABPI.
Painless, under a pressure point such as a metatarsal head, usually with diabetes.
Over a bony pressure point such as the heel or sacrum, not the gaiter area.
Rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge.

steps.x: **E. Venous ulcer.** Gaiter area + shallow, oozing + mildly painful + ABPI >0.8 = venous ulcer.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 6 month history of a weeping ulcer above her right medial malleolus. She has had varicose veins since her pregnancies and had a right calf DVT 10 years ago. Her ankles swell by the evening. Her ABPI is 0.96.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the skin around the ulcer?
o: Hairless, shiny skin with absent foot pulses
Pale skin with capillary refill of 5 seconds
questions.e: Haemosiderin from broken-down extravasated red cells stains the skin reddish-brown, with venous eczema and oedema around a venous ulcer; hairless shiny skin belongs to arterial disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: weeping ulcer above her right medial malleolus
steps.x: Chronic venous insufficiency with a gaiter ulcer: expect the skin changes of venous hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reddish-brown staining with venous eczema.

elim: Signs of arterial insufficiency; her ABPI is normal.
Poor arterial perfusion, not venous disease.
Describes a basal cell carcinoma.
Typical of pyoderma gangrenosum.

steps.x: **D. Reddish-brown staining with venous eczema.** Venous ulcer skin = brown haemosiderin staining, venous eczema, oedema, lipodermatosclerosis.

questions.stem: A 74 year old retired teacher has a 3 month history of a shallow, exudative ulcer over her left gaiter region with surrounding brown staining and pitting oedema. She has varicose veins and her legs ache after standing. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable. The nurse measures her ankle-brachial pressure index before planning dressings.
questions.q: Which is the most likely ABPI in the affected leg?
questions.e: In a venous ulcer the arterial supply is intact, so the ABPI is typically normal (above 0.8); values above 1.3 suggest calcified vessels.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
A pure venous ulcer has an intact arterial supply, so the ABPI is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Critical limb ischaemia; pulses would be absent with rest pain.
Moderate to severe arterial disease; does not fit palpable pulses and a venous picture.
Suggests mild arterial disease (a mixed picture), not simple venous disease.
Suggests calcified, non-compressible vessels, as in diabetes or CKD.

steps.x: **D. 1.0.** Venous ulcer: ABPI normal (>0.8), confirming the arteries are fine.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has had recurrent venous ulcers above both medial malleoli for 15 years. The skin of his lower calves is firm, brown and woody, and his legs narrow sharply just above the ankles, while the calves above are swollen. His foot pulses are palpable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely description of the appearance of his legs?
questions.e: Lipodermatosclerosis contracts the ankle and lower calf while oedema persists higher up, giving the inverted champagne bottle leg of chronic venous disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: narrow sharply just above the ankles
steps.x: Fibrosis narrows the ankle while the calf stays oedematous: the signature shape of chronic venous disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inverted champagne bottle.

elim: Seen in Paget's disease or rickets, not venous disease.
Describes lymphoedema or breast skin over a tumour.
Diffuse uniform swelling of lipoedema or lymphoedema without ankle tapering.
Seen in neuropathy or disuse, not with swollen calves.

steps.x: **B. Inverted champagne bottle.** Tapered fibrotic ankle + swollen calf = inverted champagne bottle.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with chronic venous insufficiency and a healing ulcer over her left medial malleolus has 2 months of itchy, red, scaly and weeping skin around both ankles. She has not used any new creams or dressings. The skin is not hot and she is well. Her temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Venous eczema is a progressive complication of chronic venous hypertension, giving itchy, scaly, weeping skin around the ankles; cellulitis is hot, unilateral and spreading.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Bilateral itchy, scaly, weeping skin in the gaiter area with venous disease and no new products: venous eczema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous eczema.

elim: Usually follows a new topical product or dressing, which she has not used.
Unilateral, hot, spreading and often with fever; this is bilateral, itchy and cool.
Well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces, not around the ankles only.
An annular scaly rash with central clearing.

steps.x: **E. Venous eczema.** Itchy, scaly gaiter skin in venous disease = venous eczema, not cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a 5 month history of a shallow ulcer above his right medial malleolus with surrounding brown staining. He fractured his right tibia 12 years ago and was treated for a right femoral DVT at the time. He also has hypertension and smoked until 10 years ago. His ABPI is 1.0.
questions.q: Which part of his history is the most likely underlying cause of this ulcer?
questions.e: A previous DVT damages venous valves (post-thrombotic syndrome), giving the chronic venous hypertension behind venous ulcers; smoking drives arterial ulcers, which a normal ABPI argues against.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: shallow ulcer above his right medial malleolus
steps.x: A venous ulcer in the same leg as an old DVT: the clot damaged the valves, causing venous hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Previous DVT.

elim: Age alone does not explain an ulcer in this one leg; the DVT does.
Causes the rare Martorell ulcer on the lateral leg, which is very painful.
A risk factor for arterial ulcers; his ABPI is normal.
The fracture itself does not ulcerate the skin years later; the DVT it caused does.

steps.x: **C. Previous DVT.** Venous ulcer risk factors: varicose veins, previous DVT, obesity, immobility.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman who works as a hairdresser has heavy, aching legs at the end of each working day and calf cramps at night. For 3 months she has had a slowly enlarging shallow ulcer above her left medial malleolus that is only mildly painful and feels better when she puts her feet up. Her foot pulses are palpable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Venous ulcers are only mildly painful and ease with elevation, with aching legs and night cramps after standing; arterial ulcer pain worsens on elevation.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: feels better when she puts her feet up
steps.x: Standing all day, aching legs and night cramps, and a mildly painful ulcer eased by elevation: venous.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous ulcer.

elim: Painful, worse on elevation and better hanging the leg down, with weak pulses.
Painless ulcer at a pressure point in a patient with diabetes.
A squamous cell carcinoma arising in a long-standing scar or ulcer.
Multiple painful punched-out ulcers with systemic features.

steps.x: **E. Venous ulcer.** Aching legs + night cramps + mildly painful ulcer eased by elevation = venous ulcer.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had a non-healing ulcer on his right lower leg for 4 months. He has varicose veins, a BMI of 34 and swollen ankles. The skin around the ulcer is reddish-brown and his ABPI is 0.98.
questions.q: Which is the most likely appearance of the ulcer?
o: Deep, punched-out ulcer on the toes with a pale base
Painless ulcer under the first metatarsal head with surrounding callus
Pearly nodule with a rolled edge
Shallow, exudative ulcer with irregular edges
Very painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge
questions.e: Venous ulcers are shallow, oozing and exudative with irregular edges and only mild pain; deep punched-out ulcers on the toes are arterial.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Venous risk factors, oedema, haemosiderin skin and a normal ABPI: a venous ulcer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Shallow, exudative ulcer with irregular edges.

elim: Describes an arterial ulcer.
Describes a neuropathic ulcer.
Describes a basal cell carcinoma.
Describes pyoderma gangrenosum.

steps.x: **D. Shallow, exudative ulcer with irregular edges.** Venous = shallow, wet, irregular; arterial = deep, dry, punched-out.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with long-standing varicose veins and ankle oedema is referred to a leg ulcer clinic with a shallow, oozing ulcer surrounded by brown, eczematous skin. Her ulcer is only mildly painful and her ABPI is 1.1. The nurse documents the site on a body chart.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the ulcer?
o: Medial gaiter region above the medial malleolus
Plantar surface of the first metatarsal head
questions.e: Venous ulcers form in the gaiter region, classically above the medial malleolus where venous pressure is highest; toe tips are arterial and the metatarsal head neuropathic.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
A venous ulcer, so it lies where venous pressure is highest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Medial gaiter region above the medial malleolus.

elim: An unusual site for venous ulcers.
A pressure point, typical of pressure ulcers.
Typical of neuropathic ulcers.
Typical of arterial ulcers.

steps.x: **C. Medial gaiter region above the medial malleolus.** Venous ulcer site: gaiter region, medial malleolus.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman has had a venous ulcer above her right medial malleolus for 8 months. For 2 days the ulcer has become more painful and a hot, red, tender area has spread 10 cm up her shin. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Calf is soft and not tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Venous ulcers are prone to secondary cellulitis: spreading warmth, redness and fever; necrotising fasciitis would cause severe pain out of proportion and systemic shock.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: hot, red, tender area has spread
Calf is soft and not tender
steps.x: An ulcer is an entry point for bacteria: spreading hot, red skin with fever is secondary infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cellulitis.

elim: Gives a swollen, tender calf, not a spreading hot red area from an ulcer.
Chronic firm brown skin without fever or acute spread.
Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, bullae or crepitus and shock.
Itchy, scaly skin without fever.

steps.x: **A. Cellulitis.** Venous ulcer + spreading hot red skin + fever = cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man had a venous ulcer above his left medial malleolus that healed after 4 months of four-layer compression bandaging. He was advised to wear compression stockings but stopped after a few weeks because they were hard to put on. Eight months later a new shallow, oozing ulcer has appeared in the same place. His ABPI is 1.05.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the ulcer has recurred?
questions.e: Venous ulcers are chronic and recur unless the venous hypertension is controlled; once healed, Class II compression stockings prevent recurrence, and he stopped them.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: healed after 4 months of four-layer compression
steps.x: The underlying venous hypertension is still there; without stockings the ulcer comes back.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Persistent venous hypertension without compression.

elim: His ABPI is normal.
A Marjolin ulcer would grow slowly with a raised edge, not recur as a shallow oozing ulcer.
Gives a deep, probing ulcer, often with diabetes.
Nothing suggests diabetes, and it causes neuropathic ulcers.

steps.x: **D. Persistent venous hypertension without compression.** Healed venous ulcer: Class II stockings for life, or it recurs.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman attends a community leg ulcer clinic with a 6 month history of an ulcer on her right lower leg. She has varicose veins and her ankles are swollen. The ulcer is shallow and moist with surrounding brown skin. Her foot pulses are palpable and her ABPI is 0.94. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Venous ulcers are the most common type of leg ulcer, caused by venous hypertension from chronic venous insufficiency; a normal ABPI excludes a mixed ulcer.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Venous hypertension from varicose veins, a moist shallow ulcer, brown skin and a normal ABPI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Venous ulcer.

elim: Painful, punched-out, with weak pulses and a low ABPI.
Would have a reduced ABPI, usually 0.5 to 0.8.
Painless pressure-point ulcer with reduced sensation.
A raised, everted edge that slowly grows.

steps.x: **E. Venous ulcer.** Commonest leg ulcer = venous; normal ABPI rules out the arterial component.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man is seen by his GP with a 3 month history of a shallow, oozing ulcer above his left medial malleolus with surrounding brown staining. He has varicose veins. He has not had a vascular assessment. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step in his assessment?
o: Skin biopsy of the ulcer edge
questions.e: Assessment of a leg ulcer starts with checking peripheral pulses, then ABPI; diagnosis is clinical supported by ABPI, and swabs are only for clinical infection.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
Before anything else, assess the arterial supply at the bedside.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palpate the foot pulses.

elim: Not a first test; reserved for planning arterial intervention.
Only for atypical or non-healing ulcers suspicious of malignancy.
All chronic ulcers grow bacteria; swab only if clinically infected.
Invasive and not part of routine assessment.

steps.x: **B. Palpate the foot pulses.** Leg ulcer: pulses first, then ABPI.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has a shallow, exudative ulcer above her right medial malleolus with surrounding haemosiderin staining, venous eczema and oedema. She has long-standing varicose veins. Her foot pulses are palpable. The junior doctor asks how the diagnosis of a venous ulcer is usually made.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: The overall gold standard for a venous ulcer is clinical diagnosis supported by ABPI; duplex ultrasound then confirms the underlying venous insufficiency.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
The features are classic; the diagnosis is clinical, with the ABPI confirming normal arteries.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical assessment supported by ABPI.

elim: Not used to diagnose a venous ulcer.
Used to exclude acute DVT, not to diagnose an ulcer.
Reserved for atypical ulcers.
Tells you about colonising bacteria, not the cause of the ulcer.

steps.x: **A. Clinical assessment supported by ABPI.** Venous ulcer diagnosis = clinical + ABPI.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man's venous ulcer above his left medial malleolus has healed with four-layer compression bandaging. He has prominent varicose veins along the medial thigh and calf. His ABPI is 1.08. He is referred to the vascular clinic to see whether his underlying venous disease can be treated to stop recurrence.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Duplex ultrasound confirms venous insufficiency by showing retrograde flow through incompetent valves and maps veins for endovenous ablation; ABPI only assesses arterial supply.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.

clues: underlying venous disease can be treated
steps.x: To plan treatment of the veins you need to see which ones reflux.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Duplex ultrasound.

elim: Already done; it assesses arteries, not venous reflux.
Invasive and replaced by ultrasound.
Images arteries, not venous reflux.
Shows bone, not veins.

steps.x: **D. Duplex ultrasound.** Venous insufficiency is confirmed and mapped with duplex ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years and stage 4 chronic kidney disease has a shallow, exudative ulcer above his right medial malleolus with brown staining. Foot pulses are hard to feel. The Doppler cuff will not occlude the ankle arteries even at high pressure.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for this result?
questions.e: An ABPI above 1.3 or arteries that will not compress suggest calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD); it is unreliable, so compression is avoided and he is referred to vascular surgery.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.

clues: will not occlude the ankle arteries
steps.x: Diabetes and CKD calcify the arterial wall, so the cuff cannot squash it and the ABPI reads falsely high.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Calcified, non-compressible arteries.

elim: Does not affect arterial compressibility.
Gives a very low ABPI, not arteries that cannot be compressed.
A falsely high ABPI cannot be read as normal.
Makes measurement uncomfortable but does not prevent arterial occlusion.

steps.x: **B. Calcified, non-compressible arteries.** ABPI >1.3 = calcified vessels: unreliable, no compression, refer.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a shallow, oozing ulcer above her left medial malleolus with surrounding haemosiderin staining. The leg ulcer nurse measures her ankle-brachial pressure index (see item resources) before deciding on treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?
o: Arterial supply adequate for four-layer compression
Calcified vessels, so compression must be avoided
Mild arterial disease needing reduced compression
Moderate arterial disease needing vascular referral
questions.e: An ABPI of 0.98 is normal, so the arterial supply is intact and four-layer compression bandaging (ABPI 0.8 to 1.3) can safely start.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
0.98 sits within 0.8 to 1.3: the arteries are normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial supply adequate for four-layer compression.

elim: That is above 1.3.
That is below about 0.3 to 0.5 with rest pain.
That is about 0.6 to 0.8.
That is about 0.5 to 0.8, with claudication.

steps.x: **A. Arterial supply adequate for four-layer compression.** ABPI 0.8 to 1.3 = safe for four-layer compression.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with a venous ulcer above her right medial malleolus had cellulitis that has settled after a course of flucloxacillin. The district nurse now plans compression bandaging. Her pulses are difficult to feel because of oedema. She has never had a vascular assessment. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting compression?
o: Duplex ultrasound of the leg veins
questions.e: ABPI must be measured before any compression to exclude arterial disease; duplex looks at veins and does not tell you if compression is safe.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
Compression is dangerous if the arteries are diseased, so measure the arterial supply first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ankle-brachial pressure index.

elim: Infection has settled and CRP does not decide on compression.
Not relevant to compression safety.
Assesses venous reflux, not whether the arteries can tolerate compression.
Infection has resolved; it does not affect compression safety.

steps.x: **A. Ankle-brachial pressure index.** No ABPI, no compression.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a 10 week history of a shallow, exudative ulcer above his left medial malleolus with brown staining and pitting oedema. He has varicose veins. There is no spreading redness. His foot pulses are palpable and his ABPI is 1.1. His temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 70 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: With ABPI 0.8 to 1.3 and no infection, four-layer compression bandaging is first-line for a venous ulcer; Class II stockings are for prevention once healed.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Arterial disease is excluded (ABPI 1.1), there is no infection, so start first-line compression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Four-layer compression bandaging.

elim: For preventing recurrence after healing, not for an active ulcer.
Treats the underlying veins later, not first-line for the ulcer.
There is no sign of infection.
Only needed with abnormal ABPI or atypical features.

steps.x: **C. Four-layer compression bandaging.** Active venous ulcer + normal ABPI = four-layer compression bandaging.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with a BMI of 36 has a venous ulcer above her right medial malleolus. Her ABPI is 1.02 and four-layer compression bandaging has started. She sits at a desk all day and rarely walks. She asks what else she can do to help it heal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional advice?
o: Bed rest until the ulcer has healed
Keep the leg hanging down when sitting
Leg elevation, walking and weight loss
Stop all exercise to protect the ulcer
questions.e: Adjuncts to compression are leg elevation, exercise (calf muscle pump) and weight reduction; immobility and dependency raise venous pressure.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.

clues: sits at a desk all day
steps.x: Anything that lowers venous pressure helps: elevation, calf pump use, and weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Leg elevation, walking and weight loss.

elim: Immobility worsens venous stasis.
Dependency raises venous pressure.
Compression must stay on continuously to work.
Calf muscle pump activity improves venous return.

steps.x: **C. Leg elevation, walking and weight loss.** Venous ulcer adjuncts: elevate, exercise, lose weight.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man's venous ulcer above his right medial malleolus healed after 3 months of four-layer compression. He now wears Class II compression stockings. Duplex ultrasound shows reflux at the saphenofemoral junction and along the great saphenous vein. His ABPI is 1.1. He asks about treatment to fix the underlying cause.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Endovenous ablation (radiofrequency or laser) is definitive treatment of the underlying superficial venous disease and lowers recurrence.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Superficial venous reflux is the cause; closing the refluxing vein treats it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Endovenous radiofrequency ablation.

elim: Antiplatelets do not treat venous reflux.
An arterial operation.
Not indicated for venous reflux without thrombosis.
The ulcer has already healed; grafting does not fix reflux.

steps.x: **B. Endovenous radiofrequency ablation.** Fix the cause: endovenous ablation of the refluxing vein.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with a venous ulcer above her left medial malleolus has 3 days of redness, warmth and tenderness spreading from the ulcer edge up her shin. She has no known drug allergies. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Flucloxacillin is first-line for an infected venous ulcer; clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic and co-amoxiclav for severe infection.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Mild to moderate cellulitis in a non-allergic patient: first-line anti-staphylococcal penicillin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Flucloxacillin.

elim: Poor activity against staphylococci and streptococci; not used for cellulitis.
Used if penicillin-allergic; she has no allergy.
Reserved for severe infection.
Covers anaerobes only.

steps.x: **D. Flucloxacillin.** Infected venous ulcer: flucloxacillin; allergic, clarithromycin; severe, co-amoxiclav.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man with a long-standing venous ulcer on his right leg has 2 days of rapidly spreading redness to the knee with swelling and pain. He is confused. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. He has no drug allergies. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Severe infection of a venous ulcer is treated with co-amoxiclav (given IV in a septic patient); flucloxacillin is first-line only for milder infection.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.

clues: rapidly spreading redness to the knee
steps.x: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension and confusion: severe infection needs broader cover.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Co-amoxiclav.

elim: For penicillin allergy, which he does not have.
An oral option for mild cellulitis in allergy.
A urinary antibiotic.
First-line for mild to moderate infection, not this severe, septic picture.

steps.x: **B. Co-amoxiclav.** Severe infected venous ulcer = co-amoxiclav.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman started four-layer compression bandaging for a venous ulcer 5 days ago. Her ABPI was not documented. She now has severe, worsening pain in the foot that keeps her awake, and her toes are pale and cool. The ulcer base has turned black. Her temperature is 37.0°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Add flucloxacillin and continue the bandage
Prescribe codeine and review in 2 weeks
Remove the bandage and arrange urgent vascular assessment
Switch to Class II compression stockings
questions.e: Rapidly worsening pain, necrosis or systemic illness in a 'venous' ulcer suggests arterial compromise; compressing a poorly perfused limb can cause critical ischaemia, so remove it and reassess urgently.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Rapidly worsening pain and necrosis under compression mean arterial compromise until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Remove the bandage and arrange urgent vascular assessment.

elim: Ignores ischaemia; infection is not the main problem.
Would worsen ischaemia.
Rapidly worsening pain and necrosis need urgent action.
Still compresses an ischaemic limb.

steps.x: **D. Remove the bandage and arrange urgent vascular assessment.** New severe pain or necrosis under compression: take it off and get vascular help.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 2 month history of a shallow, oozing ulcer above her right medial malleolus. Her ABPI is 1.05 and there is no infection. Her friend wears compression stockings and she asks whether she could use them instead of bandages because they are easier.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Four-layer bandaging is first-line for an active venous ulcer; Class II stockings are used once healed to prevent recurrence and are not appropriate during active ulceration.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Active ulcer with normal ABPI: bandaging heals it; stockings come after healing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Four-layer compression bandaging.

elim: Not appropriate during active ulceration; used once healed.
No infection.
Not first-line; compression heals most ulcers.
Treats venous eczema, not the ulcer itself.

steps.x: **B. Four-layer compression bandaging.** Active = bandages; healed = Class II stockings.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has a shallow ulcer above his left medial malleolus with haemosiderin staining and oedema. Foot pulses are faint. His ABPI is 1.45 in both legs. There is no infection. His temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: ABPI above 1.3 suggests non-compressible, calcified vessels: avoid compression and refer to vascular surgery for further arterial assessment.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
ABPI above 1.3 means calcified vessels; you cannot trust it, so do not compress.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Referral to vascular surgery.

elim: Compression must be avoided until arterial disease is excluded.
Unsafe: a falsely high ABPI may hide arterial disease.
There is no infection.
Delays treatment of an active ulcer.

steps.x: **D. Referral to vascular surgery.** ABPI >1.3 = no compression, refer to vascular.
